Mushroom.
DIFFICULTY
Easy
1/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Spring / Summer / Autumn / Winter

This guide covers cultivated button and chestnut mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus), grown in prepared mushroom compost away from direct sun. Fresh ready-spawned kits in bags, buckets or boxes are the simplest route to small crops while outdoor beds are quiet. Check the start-by date and begin promptly: pre-started kits may already be largely colonised. Follow the supplier’s stages, casing and temperatures. Preparing compost from raw ingredients needs controlled composting and conditioning; other mushroom species need different substrates and conditions.

Key risks
Pests

Mushroom flies can infest compost and damage developing mushrooms.

Contaminating moulds

Contaminating fungi can discolour mushroom substrate or distort and decay developing mushrooms.

Poor cropping

Slow colonisation or stalled cropping may result from unsuitable temperatures, moisture or ventilation.

Start with prepared mushroom compost.

A fresh ready-spawned kit is the simplest route for small quantities.

Keep conditions steady.

Avoid direct sun, temperature extremes and waterlogged casing.

Soil & preparation
Button mushrooms need prepared mushroom compost, not garden soil. Buy fresh spawned compost or a kit. Commercial compost often uses straw, manure and gypsum, processed before spawning.
Home preparation needs initial composting plus controlled pasteurisation and conditioning to remove ammonia. Looks or a fixed number of turns cannot prove readiness; use a complete tested method and suitable equipment.
After colonisation, button mushrooms need a moist casing layer. Follow the kit’s casing material and timing; keep moist, never saturated. Other species may not need casing.
Establishing the crop
Start with spawned compost
Maintain moisture
Start the kit 

Use fresh, ready-spawned button-mushroom compost in its bag, bucket or box. Stand it in shade away from direct sun.

Add the casing 

Follow the kit instructions for when to add the casing layer. Moisten it lightly and keep it damp without soaking the compost.

Looking after the crop
Follow the kit temperatures for spawn growth and cropping. Keep the kit ventilated and out of direct sun.
Colonising compost gives off heat. Check the supplier’s temperature range to avoid overheating.
Many button kits crop at 61–64°F; follow the supplier’s range. Water casing carefully to keep lightly moist, never saturated.
Harvesting & storage
Pick before the veil opens for closed buttons, later for open caps. Flushes alternate with rests; timing and duration depend on kit and conditions.
Twist buttons gently to lift without much disturbance. Trim dirty bases and remove broken remnants; refill holes with suitable casing if the kit advises.
After the last crop, compost healthy spent substrate or use as soil improver. Weather first near seedlings/salt-sensitive plants: mushroom compost can contain high soluble salts. Start with fresh prepared material.
Keep the casing moist between flushes. Once cropping ends, empty, wash, rinse and dry reusable containers.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Pests	Small flies appear; larvae damage mushrooms or compost.	Use clean equipment, exclude flies and remove spent or infested material.
Contaminating moulds	Unusual coloured mould or misshapen, decaying mushrooms.	Isolate affected kits; ask the supplier and discard contaminated material.
Poor cropping	Spawn runs poorly or cropping stalls.	Check kit temperature, moisture and airflow; avoid sun and saturation.
Final tips

Use fresh kits and check the supplier’s start-by date rather than storing them indefinitely.

Grow from identified cultivated spawn; do not treat an unknown mushroom appearing nearby as part of the crop.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
67
